title: Answer of Google LLC in response to pleadings re PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s filing to establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service under ER26-3515.

documents.name: Answer of Google LLC - ER26-3515-000.pdf
documents.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                               BEFORE THE
                  FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.                        )               Docket No. ER26-3515-000
                                                    )
                                                    )
                                                    )
                                                    )

                                    ANSWER OF GOOGLE LLC

       Pursuant to Rule 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”), 1 Google LLC (“Google”) hereby moves to

answer and answers the pleadings filed in this proceeding. PJM is at a crossroads. The record of

this proceeding confirms that its resource adequacy challenges are real and, if left unaddressed,

will degrade reliability for all customers. And although some customers, including Google, are

making the critical investments needed to serve their load growth, that is far from universal. As a

result, there is every reason to believe that forecasted demand for capacity will continue growing

faster than supply. Nevertheless, PJM has offered a proposal, Interim Resource Adequacy Service

(“IRAS”), that will make the situation worse. It will chill investment and undermine efforts by

companies, like Google, that are committed to bringing their own new capacity to PJM.

Accordingly, the Commission should use this proceeding to put PJM back on course to a resource-

adequate future. In particular, as discussed below, it should require PJM to adopt an interruptible

capacity service similar to what exists in the natural gas transportation context under the Natural

Gas Act (“NGA”). This service will provide a mechanism for balancing supply and demand

without undermining investment in new capacity in the way IRAS would.



    1 18 C.F.R. § 385.213 (2026).
         Google agrees with the principle underlying IRAS: “New Large Loads that do not bring

sufficient new capacity to offset their expected demand should be subject to curtailment prior to

other firm wholesale customers during tight system conditions.” 2 Consistent with that view and

Google’s commitment to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, Google is actively procuring new

capacity to cover its projected load growth in PJM and will submit documentation to PJM showing

that it has brought its own new capacity (“BYONC”) to reduce or offset its obligations under the

Reliability Backstop Procurement (“RBP”) construct. 3 For that reason, Google’s interest in this

proceeding is not to avoid paying for new capacity. Rather, Google’s concern is that IRAS will

make it less likely that Google and other large customers can bring their own new capacity and

avoid curtailment to a market governed by IRAS.

        In addition, Google agrees with commenters arguing that reform is necessary. Under the

status quo, capacity market demand is already exceeding supply and it is likely to continue to do

so in the future as Load Serving Entities (“LSEs”) sign up additional firm retail customers pursuant

to applicable state law. A situation in which demand for firm service regularly exceeds supply is

an untenable outcome. After all, while those retail arrangements are governed by state law, the

physical limitations on the system are not. The capacity market cannot supply more capacity than

exists in reality. But the PJM tariff does not provide LSEs with an option to procure anything

other than firm capacity, meaning that, when supply exceeds demand, LSEs are left trying to try

to procure something that does not exist. An interruptible service—akin to what exists in the gas

transportation context and building upon what the Commission required in the PJM Co -Location

Order—is the missing link that would allow supply and demand to clear in the capacity market


     2 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Protest of Google LLC, Docket No. ER26-3515-000, at 1 (filed Sep. 3, 2026)
(“Google Protest”).
     3 See PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 196 FERC ¶ 61,245 (2026).



                                                         -2-
 without creating pervasive uncertainty that would interfere with investment in new capacity. In

the absence of such an interruptible service, PJM is providing what amounts to non -firm service

without a non-firm service class in the tariff. That result, Google submits, is unjust and

unreasonable.

         IRAS, by contrast, is not the solution. The overwhelming weight of the record compiled

in this proceeding indicates that IRAS is, for myriad reasons, illegal, ineffectual, and otherwise

deeply flawed. 4 It would, therefore, cast a long shadow over resource procurement in the region,

meaning that “the result of IRAS will be less investment in new capacity in PJM—the exact

opposite of what the region needs.” 5 An order accepting IRAS will cause resource adequacy in

PJM to deteriorate further.

         The Commission must now guide PJM back on course. To do so, it should use the logic

of its recent PJM Co-Location Orders6 to require PJM to establish an interruptible service in the

capacity market similar to what exists in the gas transportation context. 7 It has two viable options

to do so. First, it could reject IRAS with guidance on how PJM can reform the proposal to actually

improve resource adequacy in PJM. 8 Any such order should make clear to PJM that it cannot

condition the quality of wholesale service on retail customer characteristics and that a successor



     4 Infra section II.A.

     5 Google Protest at 2.

     6 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 193 FERC ¶ 61,217 (2025) (“PJM Co-Location Order”).

     7 Duke Energy Trading & Mktg., L.L.C. v. FERC, 315 F.3d 377, 378-79 (D.C. Cir. 2003).

     8 This would be consistent with what PJM has requested the Commission to do if the Commission rejects IRAS.
See PJM Answer at 5 (“PJM respectfully requests that, to the extent the Commission rejects any element of this filing,
the Commission either direct prescriptive changes to be implemented on compliance or provide guidance to aid PJM
and stakeholders to develop a just and reasonable approach. The issues outlined herein are simply too important, and
the timing too critical, for PJM and its stakeholders to have to guess in such a case as to what the Commission would
find acceptable.”).



                                                             -3-
 construct to IRAS must create the conditions necessary to facilitate investment in new capacity,

not stymie it. Specifically, it should create a class of interruptible service governed by transparent,

clear rules that provide the regulatory certainty necessary to facilitate the at-risk investments that

are the bedrock of a market-based approach to ensure resource adequacy.

        Alternatively, the Commission could take the reins and begin the process to “transform”

this section 205 into a section 206 proceeding. Although in a typical proceeding under section 205

of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), the Commission generally “undertakes ‘an essentially passive

and reactive role’ and restricts itself to evaluating the confined proposal,” 9 the U.S. Court of

Appeals for the D.C. Circuit has recognized an exception to that general rule. Specifically, the

court has explained that the Commission may transform a section 205 proceeding into a section

206 proceeding and impose its own replacement rate provided that it makes three findings.

“[F]irst, it must conclude under § [205] that the [public utility] failed to carry its burden of proof

that the proposed rate was just and reasonable; second, it must itself demonstrate that the default

position, the prior rate, is no longer just and reasonable; and third, it must establish

that its substitute rate is just and reasonable.” 10

        The record in this proceeding shows how the Commission can readily make all three

findings: (1) for the reasons explained in Google’s initial protest and throughout the record, IRAS

is unjust and unreasonable, unduly discriminatory, and in excess of the Commission’s jurisdiction;



    9 Advanced Energy Mgmt. All. v. FERC, 860 F.3d 656, 662 (D.C. Cir. 2017) (quoting City of Winnfield v. FERC,
744 F.2d 871, 875-76 (D.C. Cir. 1984)).
     10 W. Res., Inc. v. FERC, 9 F.3d 1568, 1579 (D.C. Cir. 1993) (citing the parallel provisions of the Natural Gas
Act); While Western Resources addressed sections 4 and 5 of the Natural Gas Act, its reasoning and framework
nevertheless apply equally to FPA cases involving section 205 proceedings that the Commission converts into section
206 proceedings because “the relevant provisions of the [NGA and FPA] ‘are in all material respects substantially
identical.’” Arkansas Louisiana Gas Co. v. Hall, 453 U.S. 571, 577 n.7 (1981) (quoting FPC v. Sierra Pacific Power
Co., 350 U.S. 348, 353 (1956)); see also Monongahela Power Co., 164 FERC ¶ 61,217, at P 17 (2018) (applying
Western Resources in an a proceeding that was initiated under FPA section 205).

                                                            -4-
      (2) the status quo is also unjust and unreasonable as LSEs are signing up more new retail customers

     than the region can reliably serve yet the PJM tariff lacks any mechanism for equilibrating supply

     and demand in the capacity market; and (3) as Google explained in its initial protest, “there are

     ample alternative avenues through which PJM, in cooperation with the States, could facilitate the

     goals underlying IRAS, rather than impeding them,” 11 including the development of an

     interruptible service, modeled on what exists for natural gas transportation, that provides clear and

     transparent rules for determining which customers take interruptible service as well as when and

     how they will be interrupted to ensure supply and demand remain balanced. To implement this

     option, the Commission could find that all of IRAS is unjust and unreasonable or it could accept

     only the Large Load Registry.          Either way, it would simultaneously initiate a section 206

     proceeding regarding the existing tariff (Western Resources Step 2 above) and potential

     replacement rates (Western Resources Step 3 above) and consolidate the record of this proceeding

     into that new one. 12

            It bears reiterating: Google’s interest in this proceeding is to ensure that PJM has a

     functioning resource adequacy construct that provides the incentives necessary to develop

     sufficient new capacity to meet demand in PJM over the short-, medium-, and long-term. IRAS is

     emphatically not that. Accordingly, Google urges the Commission to assert its leadership on these

     issues and put PJM back on course.

I.      MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

            Although the Commission’s procedural rules generally do not allow answers to answers,




         11 Google Protest at 16.

         12 See Tennessee Gas Pipeline Co.v. FERC, 860 F.2d 446, 456 (D.C. Cir. 1988); W. Res., Inc. v. FERC, 9 F.3d
     at 1579; Monongahela Power Co., 164 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 17.

                                                              -5-
   the Commission may permit them for good cause. 13 The Commission frequently accepts answers

  that clarify the issues before the Commission, ensure a complete record, or otherwise assist the

  Commission in its decision-making.14 Google therefore respectfully requests that the Commission

  accept this answer, which will assist the Commission with its decision-making by setting forth the

  justification for the Commission action under the Western Resources framework, discussed above.

II.   ANSWER

           As Google explained in its initial protest, PJM is correct that the demand for electricity is

  outpacing supply, and reforms are necessary to manage periods in which demand exceeds supply

  and to incentivize the development of the new capacity to prevent tho se imbalances in the future.

  But IRAS would only make things worse. As an overwhelming majority of commenters pointed

  out, IRAS is both illegal and likely to be counterproductive. Rather than incentivizing New Large

  Loads to contract with new capacity, it will chill such investment and further erode resource

  adequacy in the region. That uncertainty is the result of both IRAS’s patent legal deficiencies,

  which provide ample bases for it to be overturned on appeal, and the fact that PJM lacks authority

  to dictate retail curtailment priority, which means that IRAS will not provide the regulatory

  certainty that is necessary to incentivize investment in new capacity.

           The Commission must either reject IRAS with guidance to PJM to establish a legally

  durable approach that includes a clear and transparent category interruptible service that does not



        13 18 C.F.R. § 385.213(a)(2) (“An answer may not be made to a protest, an answer, a motion for oral argument,
  or a request for rehearing, unless otherwise ordered by the decisional authority.”).
       14 See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 182 FERC ¶ 61,073, at P 13 (2023) (accepting answers to answers that
  “provided information that assisted us in our decision-making process”); New Fortress Energy LLC, 174 FERC
  61,207, at P 7 (2021) (accepting answers because they provided information that assisted the Commission’s
  decisionmaking process); Alaska Gasline Dev. Corp., 171 FERC ¶ 61,134, at P 7 (2020) (accepting answers that
  “clarify the concerns raised and provide information that has assisted in our decision making”); Saltville Gas Storage
  Co., L.L.C., 164 FERC ¶ 61,212, at P 2 n.6 (2018) (accepting answers that “assist the Commission in understanding
  the issues raised, and will ensure a complete record”).

                                                               -6-
 target individual retail customers or take the reins itself to do the same pursuant to the D.C.

Circuit’s decision in Western Resources by “transforming” this section 205 proceeding into one

under section 206. 15

        The Commission can satisfy all three Western Resources conditions here. First, it should

reject IRAS because it exceeds the Commission’s jurisdiction under the FPA and has not been

shown to be just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. Google explained

these points in its initial protest, and the record established so far in this proceeding only confirms

the point. The one possible exception is the Large Load Registry, which could play a valuable

information-sharing role without transgressing the FPA’s jurisdictional lines and could be severed

from the rest of the filing consistent with PJM’s statements in its transmittal letter and the

principles in NRG.16

        Second, despite demand for firm capacity outpacing supply, there is no option in PJM’s

tariff allowing LSEs to take interruptible service. The absence of any interruptible service, and

the resulting imbalance in the supply and demand for firm capacity, is eroding system reliability

and will degrade the quality of firm service because PJM will inevitably have to manage supply

and demand through the use of emergency procedures and curtailment of customers attempting to

take firm service. In addition to degrading the quality of Commission jurisdictional service, it also

creates uncertainty that impairs investment in new capacity needed for PJM to eventually escape

the current resource adequacy crisis. Accordingly, the fact that the PJM tariff lacks a permanent,




     15 W. Res., Inc. v. FERC, 9 F.3d at 1579; see also Monongahela Power Co., 164 FERC ¶ 61,217 at P 17.

     16 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Proposal to Establish Interim Resource Adequacy Service and a Large Load
Registry to Address System Reliability, Docket No. ER26-3515-000, at 9 (filed Aug. 13, 2026) (“Transmittal”); NRG
Power Mktg., LLC v. FERC, 862 F.3d 108, 114 (D.C. Cir. 2017) (holding that the Commission has “some authority
to propose modifications to a utility’s [FPA section 205] proposal if the utility consents to the modifications”).

                                                           -7-
 clearly defined service option through which an LSE can procure interruptible, non -capacity

backed service renders the PJM tariff unjust and unreasonable.

       Third, the Commission should adopt a replacement rate that establishes an interruptible

service option through which an LSE can elect to serve load on a non -firm basis. Such service

would not be capacity-backed, and PJM would not procure capacity to serve it. Instead, load

taking interruptible service could consume electricity when there is sufficient capacity on the

system, subject to defined triggers to interrupt the provision of electricity as conditions tighten and

before emergency procedures are triggered. This service would be highly similar to interruptible

service in the gas transportation context, which would allow additional demand to be served while

preserving priority for firm customers. It would also build on the reasoning underlying the

Commission’s recent PJM Co-Location Order where it created interim Network Integration

Transmission Service (“NITS”) to address a similar concept.

       PJM should define this service in its tariff, including when it is available and when PJM

would direct LSEs to curtail participating load. Curtailment would be a condition of interruptible

service, triggered before emergency procedures become necessary.              States would then be

responsible for determining which retail customers take interruptible retail service. That approach

both solves the basic supply and demand problem—because PJM knows to interrupt the

interruptible customers when demand exceeds supply—and puts states in position to determine

which customers qualify for firm service and which do not. For example, the states could

determine whether data centers can receive firm service only if they bring their own new capacity

and customers, including data centers, would have the certainty they need to make investments in

such new capacity because the regulator imposing the requirement also has authority over the

curtailment priority. In that way, this approach would address the basic motivation behind IRAS



                                                     -8-
 without the self-defeating uncertainty that it would create. Additionally, to address a potential

supply shortfall in the near term, PJM should establish a framework for curtailing large loads,

including those with firm service, prior to other retail customers during emergency conditions

when PJM is approaching a broad Manual Load Dump.

        A. The Record Confirms that PJM Has Not Satisfied Its FPA Section 205 Burden

        Google explained in its initial protest that IRAS falls well short of meeting PJM’s burden

under section 205 to show that its proposal meets the just and reasonable standard and is not unduly

discriminatory. Instead, it is fatally flawed in several respects. First, IRAS exceeds the

Commission’s authority because it aims at, targets, and is impermissibly tethered to the retail

sphere.17 Second, IRAS unduly discriminates on the basis of retail customer characteristics that

are beyond the Commission’s jurisdiction to consider and, separately, for reasons that have nothing

to do with the resource adequacy concerns that PJM is trying to address (e.g., when the large load

began operating). 18 Finally, IRAS is unjust and unreasonable because PJM would require IRAS

curtailment before deploying demand response resources that have agreed to be curtailable and

because PJM cannot ensure that New Large Loads that bring new capacity will receive firm

service.19   Each of those several issues would provide an appellate court with sufficient

justification to overturn an order accepting the IRAS proposal.

        Were there any doubts about the legality of IRAS, the Commission need only look at the

pleadings in this docket, which overwhelmingly confirm that IRAS has not been shown to be just

and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential. Indeed, the overwhelming majority


    17 Google Protest at 8-11; see Oneok, Inc. v. Learjet, Inc., 575 U.S. 373, 385 (2015) (“Oneok”); FERC v. Elec.
Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260, 282 (2016) (“EPSA”); Hughes v. Talen Energy Mktg., LLC, 578 U.S. 150, 166
(2016) (“Hughes”).
    18 Google Protest at 11-13.

    19 Id. at 13-16.



                                                          -9-
 of entities participating in this proceeding—utilities, independent power producers, data center

operators, consumer advocates, industry trade groups, state public utility commissions, and

individual retail customers—all oppose IRAS in whole or part. Of the roughly 40 parties that filed

initial pleadings in the docket, only a few embrace the IRAS proposal and recommend that the

Commission accept it as proposed. The number and quality of the protests provide compelling

evidence both that PJM has not met its burden with respect to IRAS and that any order accepting

it would face strong challenges on appeal. Simply put, the record in this proceeding provides

more-than-ample evidence for the Commission to conclude that IRAS exceeds the Commission’s

jurisdiction and has not been shown to be just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or

preferential.

       Although the record reflects overwhelming opposition to IRAS, a handful of answers now

seek to resuscitate the moribund case for accepting it. Google appreciates that those answers

reflect a genuine belief that IRAS will respond to the very real practical challenges caused by load

growth that outstrips supply. Nevertheless, as explained below and in Google’s initial protest,

accepting IRAS would make matters worse by creating pervasive uncertainty that will exacerbate

the region’s resource adequacy shortfall. Although Google agrees that PJM and the Commission

should do something, it is critical that PJM and the Commission do the right thing, lest PJM’s

resource adequacy situation deteriorate further at a time when PJM can least afford it.

       Google agrees that PJM is facing the prospect of a serious resource adequacy shortfall and

that New Large Loads must step up and cover that capacity shortfall, consistent with the Ratepayer

Protection Pledge. As noted above, that is exactly what Google is doing as it expands its operations

in PJM. Google has also made clear that New Large Loads that do not offset their demand with

new capacity should be curtailed prior to other firm wholesale customers when system conditions



                                                   -10-
 warrant. Accordingly, when it comes to Google, it is incorrect to suggest that opposition to IRAS

“fl[ies] in the face of commitments . . . already made in the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, and [is]

essentially an argument that the new capacity needed to serve data centers must be paid for by all

PJM customers through higher capacity market prices rather than by the actual cost-causers.’” 20

Instead, Google opposes IRAS because of its potential to exacerbate the region’s resource

adequacy issues, harming all PJM customers. Far from evincing any weakness in Google’s

commitment to the Ratepayer Protection Pledge, our opposition reflects our commitment to well-

functioning and rational markets as one of the central pillars by which the industry can realize the

goals of the Pledge.

       Below, Google addresses the key points in the answers filed to date and explains why they

do not call into question the clear consensus among the initial comments that IRAS is

fundamentally flawed and must be rejected.

                 1. Jurisdiction

       IRAS exceeds the Commission’s jurisdiction. The arguments to the contrary do not wrestle

with the critical jurisdictional arguments, instead slaying strawmen and assuming away IRAS’s

fundamental flaws. Indeed, many of those arguments are variations on th e theme that, because

PJM does not direct the curtailment of individual retail customers, IRAS must not exceed the

Commission’s jurisdiction. For instance, PJM contends that “the issue of jurisdiction is about

which entity gets to identify the retail customers who ultimately respond to PJM’s directives to

reduce load.” 21 But the FPA does not so rigidly elevate form over substance in the way some

parties suggest. Instead, courts have “emphasize[d] the importance of considering the target” of



    20 Gov. Shapiro Answer at 5.

    21 PJM Answer at 29.



                                                   -11-
 the regulation in question when considering jurisdictional challenges under the FPA. 22 It is that

inquiry that recognizes the fact that the federal and state spheres of jurisdiction under the FPA are

not “hermetically sealed” 23 and, if not properly policed, a federal or state regulation that purports

to address a jurisdictionally appropriate matter can, in fact, regulate a matter within the other’s

exclusive jurisdiction.

       IRAS’s target is evident from its very structure. IRAS conditions the quality of wholesale

service on the characteristics of retail customers. Specifically, under IRAS, PJM would identify

for each zone or area the Eligible New Large Load Amounts—i.e., the quantity of New Large Load

demand that is not offset by new capacity. 24 When system conditions warrant, PJM would instruct

(“Electric Distributors”) EDs to curtail load in amounts equal to or less than the ED’s Eligible New

Large Load Amount. 25 In other words, the amount of load shed under IRAS depends entirely and

exclusively on the characteristics of the retail load in each zone or area. Retail customers are “the

mechanism through which the rule operates.”26 That is the purpose of IRAS, not some unintended

byproduct. To see that clearly, it is worth considering what would happen if the IRAS MW load

reduction in each zone or area was not determined by, and thus tethered to, individual retail

customer characteristics. In that hypothetical, PJM would have no mechanism for determining the

amount of load to reduce in a given footprint, and, simply put, IRAS would cease being IRAS. The

retail customer targeting is therefore the defining feature of the proposal.




    22 Oneok, 575 U.S. at 385; EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282 (citing Oneok, 575 U.S. at 385).

    23 EPSA, 577 U.S. at 281.

    24 Transmittal at 69.

    25 See, e.g., id. at 86.

    26 EPSA, 577 U.S. at 283.



                                                      -12-
          In arguing to the contrary, PJM fundamentally misrepresents the Supreme Court’s

“targeting” inquiry, arguing that “[w]hether such a rule ‘targets’ retail or wholesale customers

turns on the justification for the rule, not on whether or the extent to which the rule affects or even

compels action of retail or wholesale customers.” 27 When it comes to determining whether a rate

is jurisdictionally permissible under the FPA, the dispositive question is how it works in practice,

not the relevant public utility’s transmittal letter. While the justification a public utility provides

can shed light on how the tariff works, the jurisdictional inquiry turns on what is actually on file

with the Commission. 28 After all, if the justification were all that matters, FERC could force a

public utility to adopt time-of-use retail rates by listing their salutary effects on the wholesale

market.

         The Court’s precedents confirm that is how the FPA works. In EPSA, the Court began by

examining how “demand response works” and concluding that it was an exclusively wholesale

construct before observing that the Commission’s justification was “all about and only about” the

wholesale market. 29 Similarly, in Hughes, although Maryland’s justification was to encourage

construction of new in-state generation,30 that did “not save” the program because “States may not

seek to achieve ends, however legitimate, through regulatory means that intrude on FERC’s

authority.” 31




     27 PJM Answer at 18-19.

     28 See 16 U.S. Code § 824d(c) (“[E]very public utility shall file with the Commission . . . and shall keep open in
convenient form and place for public inspection schedules showing all rates and charges for any transmission or sale
subject to the jurisdiction of the Commission, and the classifications, practices, and regulations affecting such rates
and charges.”).
     29 EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282.

     30 Hughes v. Talen Energy Mktg., LLC, 578 U.S. 150, 158 (2016).

     31 Id. at 163-64.



                                                             -13-
        Applying that framework here, the fact that PJM’s transmittal letter uses “reliability,” 32

“resource adequacy,” 33 “reserve requirements,”34 and other wholesale-market verbiage cannot

make IRAS legal. That is because no number of synonyms for reliability can cure the fact that

retail characteristics, including retail customer size and retail customer interconnection and ramp

rates, are what determine whether and how IRAS applies. As Google explained in its opening

protest, it is not the wholesale-market growth rates that determine whether IRAS applies;

wholesale-market growth is irrelevant. Consider the following two examples. First, IRAS would

not apply to an ED that grows by 1,000 one-MW increments while it would apply to an ED that

grows by 50 MW due to a single customer. Second, an ED that adds an otherwise Eligible New

Large Load on May 31, 2027 would not be subject to IRAS, while an identical ED that adds an

Eligible New Large Load on June 1, 2027 would be. In other words, while an ED’s aggregate load

growth is the demand-side metric relevant to resource adequacy, it is not the focus of IRAS and

does not determine whether IRAS applies. That is what matters because, when it comes to FPA

jurisdiction, actions speak louder than words.

       PJM also suggests that IRAS must be jurisdictionally sound because it would regulate

issues at the confluence of federal and state jurisdiction, arguing that “entities that seek rejection

of the IRAS proposal on jurisdictional grounds conveniently overlook the fact that integrating

large loads in a manner that (1) ensures reliability; (2) allows for these loads to interconnect to the

system; and (3) protects existing ratepayers, is a responsibility shared between the states and

PJM.”35 Google agrees that both the Commission and the states have important roles to play in


    32 PJM Answer at 21 (quoting Transmittal at 6).

    33 Id. (quoting Transmittal at 3).

    34 Id. (quoting Transmittal at 2).

    35 Id. at 3.



                                                      -14-
 addressing the issues in this docket. 36 But the fact that both the Commission and states have an

important role to play does not give PJM license to redraw the FPA’s jurisdictional line to suit its

preferences.

         Other specific arguments advanced in defense of IRAS fare no better. For example, parties

contend that IRAS does not “target retail customers by making the characteristics of the retail

customer the basis for a curtailment obligation.” 37 But the same Answer disproves this argument,

explaining that “PJM proposes to limit the total MWs of load reduction in a zone or area based on

the share of new large loads . . . that have failed to meet their capacity needs through BYONC or

capacity procured pursuant to Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP) rules.” 38 Similarly, the

Public Interest Organizations argue that “PJM will respect jurisdictional boundaries by directing

IRAS Actions at the wholesale level. PJM will never curtail individual retail customers—instead,

it uses the Registry and results from the most recent BRA to designate megawatt quantities of

IRAS curtailment by zone.” 39 But here too, the quoted language proves that the opposite is true

because the individual retail customer characteristics in the Large Load Registry are what trigger

the wholesale curtailments under IRAS, illustrating how IRAS is targeted at retail custo mers. In

short, no one in this proceeding has credibly shown that IRAS is “all about, and only about” the

wholesale market. 40 Instead, as even statements from supporters of IRAS demonstrate, retail

customer characteristics are the trigger for IRAS, which illustrates how IRAS targets the retail



     36 See infra section II.C. (explaining that the Commission could direct PJM to amend its tariff to establish a
federal interruptible service framework that would accommodate state retail-level tariffs).
     37 Gov. Shapiro Answer at 7 (cleaned up) (quoting Google Protest at 8 -9).

     38 Id. at 8; see id. (IRAS “[d]uly target[s] load reductions in zones or areas with non-capacity backed new large

loads . . . .” (emphasis added)).
     39 PIOs Comments at 19.

     40 EPSA, 577 U.S. at 282.



                                                            -15-
 market by creating the sort of impermissible “tether” to the retail market that cannot be remedied

by its wholesale market effects. 41

         The same goes for arguments that IRAS is about addressing transmission zones with

capacity shortfalls. For example, parties attempt to recast IRAS as “focus[ing] on zones or areas

projected to have capacity shortfalls in real-time—through the existence of non-capacity backed

large loads in the planning horizon.” 42 But those descriptions overlook the defining feature of

IRAS: how PJM determines the amount of load to be reduced under IRAS. That determination

depends entirely on the extent to which certain retail customers offset their demand with new

capacity. IRAS does not focus on areas projected to have capacity shortfalls; only on areas with

retail customers that qualify as Eligible New Large Loads. As explained above, a zone could have

a GW capacity shortfall and be exempt from IRAS if its load growth is in the form of 1,000 one-

MW loads (or, indeed, 20 49-MW loads), while another zone that does not have a shortfall but has

one New Large Load that did not bring new capacity would be subject to IRAS. Put differently,

under IRAS, an LSE or an ED could be net long, with sufficient capacity to serve all of the loads

in its footprint, but if a New Large Load comes online without offsetting capacity, that LSE/ED

would still receive a curtailment instruction. As the above hypothetical confirms, yet again, IRAS

is about the transmission zone’s retail customers, not about its capacity shortfall.

certainty needed to make long-term investments in new capacity. In addition, the creation of an

interruptible class of service would also prevent the degradation of firm service by providing a tool

to manage supply and demand without triggering emergency procedures and, if necessary, a

manual load dump.

        An interruptible service class would resolve several of the fundamental flaws in IRAS. For

example, because the service class would be available to LSEs directly, there would be no need

for IRAS’s targeting of retail customer characteristics or, for that matter, any tethering to the retail

market whatsoever. 94 In addition, it would also address the price formation and retail ratemaking

concerns associated with IRAS’s proposal to remove load from the VRR curve, but nevertheless

charge and rebate capacity costs for customers that are subject to IRAS and ultimate ly curtailed.

Because the service class is interruptible and, therefore, not backed by firm capacity, there would

be no need to include this load in the capacity market at all or provide compensation to retail

customers when it is interrupted.

        Critically, a federal interruptible service framework would also establish the necessary

foundation for BYONC to work in practice. That is because any BYONC requirement could be

enshrined in the state retail-level tariffs that by determining the rules and criteria by which retail

          In addition, as part of the replacement rate, PJM would need to establish clear rules

governing how state-designated interruptible loads are reflected in the relevant programs under its

jurisdiction, including capacity procurement requirements, capacity obligations, and transmission

planning. Interruptible loads should be included in PJM’s gross load forecast and operating models

III.   CONCLUSION

          Demand for capacity in PJM is exceeding supply, creating a significant resource adequacy

   shortfall. Accepting IRAS would only worsen the situation. Instead, the Commission should use

   this proceeding as the jumping off point to create a new interruptible capacity service. In so doing,

   the Commission would put in place the conditions to manage the existing capacity shortfall while

   also establishing the foundation for States to exercise their retail authority to impose a legally

   durable BYONC obligation on New Large Loads should they choose to do so. Accordingly, a new

   interruptible service would provide a legally durable path to achieve the goals underlying IRAS

   without the self-defeating uncertainty that IRAS would create.
